dispute_change_summary: The 2003 Technical Amendment, which builds on a procedure in the Section XXII arbitration framework (a tribunal, awards and last best offer arbitration) not found in the 1992 text, adds last best offer arbitration of compact amendments when a tribunal finds a party failed to negotiate in good faith, and lets a dispute dismissed from court for lack of a sovereign immunity waiver be treated as an arbitrable XXII.A dispute. The earlier compact provided written notice, a meeting within 30 days, and after 90 days any available remedy, with mediation or arbitration only by mutual agreement.

dispute_summary: Disputes are resolved by arbitration under CPR rules unless the parties choose negotiation, mediation or court (Section XXII.D), with a last-best-offer format when the parties agree.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides that any claim or dispute arising out of the compact is resolved by binding arbitration under CPR rules (last, best offer format unless opted out, final and unappealable except on 9 U.S.C. § 10 grounds), unless the parties agreed to negotiation, mediation or court. The earlier compact provided written notice, a meeting within 30 days, and after 90 days any available remedy, with mediation or arbitration only by mutual agreement.

The 2019 amendment deletes Section XXII.A.11 (the last best offer arbitration of a substitute compact amendment tied to a Secretarial determination) and adds a rule sending disputes over the new revenue-loss payment adjustment to Section XXII, with the payment adjustment applied pending resolution. The rest of the 2006 dispute clause is not amended.

dispute_summary: Disputes over minimum internal control standards and rules of play for event wagering are resolved by arbitration under Section XXXIV.D, with the arbitrator applying a standard tied to what the State and other Wisconsin tribes have agreed, and the compact's general dispute clause is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 amendment adds that disputes over minimum internal control standards and rules of play for event and remote wagering are arbitrated under Section XXXIV.D, except XXXIV.D.3, with the arbitrator deciding whether the proposed controls are substantially the same as those agreed to by the State and other Wisconsin tribes. The general Section XXII dispute clause of the 2006 compact is not amended.

dispute_summary: The compact has no negotiation, arbitration or court process for disputes; its only mechanism is default: a party in failure may be terminated by the other after ninety days written notice if the breach is not agreed to be remedied and is not in fact remedied, and either party may terminate on 120 days notice.

Disputes over regulations are decided by a single JAMS arbitrator under Comprehensive Arbitration Rules, and the arbitrator's order takes effect on issuance with review waived; the general Section 13 dispute clause is not in the excerpt.

The compact provides for arbitration of disputes, with the majority decision of the arbitrator(s) final, binding and unappealable and a failure to comply with the award treated as a breach of the compact; the arbitration body is not named in the excerpt, and U.S. District Courts have jurisdiction over actions to enjoin class III gaming conducted in violation of the compact.

The compact provides for written notice, a meeting within ten days, and arbitration in Arizona if the dispute is not resolved within thirty days, with one agreed arbitrator or a panel of three whose third member the American Arbitration Association appoints if the two cannot agree; the majority decision is final, binding and unappealable, and U.S. District Courts have jurisdiction over actions to enjoin class III gaming in violation of the compact.
dispute_change_summary: The 1992 excerpt begins mid-arbitration (arbitrator qualifications, costs, and a final, binding and unappealable decision), and the 1993 excerpt begins with the procedure's opening subsections. The 1992 notice and meeting steps are not in the excerpt, so the procedures cannot be fully compared. Both excerpts show a final, binding and unappealable arbitration decision and an equal cost-sharing clause.

The 2003 excerpt mentions dispute-resolution procedures only in a list of required ordinance provisions (subsection (D)) and does not show a dispute process in the compact. The 1993 procedure's arbitration steps are visible in the earlier excerpt, so the comparison cannot be made.

The 2009 Agreement to Amend lists nine compact sections it amends (Sections 2(n), 3(d), 3(d)(8), 3(m), 4(d), 5(i) and (n), 6(g), 7(g) and 12(e)), none of them Section 15. Paragraph 11 states that the agreement is subject to the compact's dispute-resolution provisions in Section 15, so the earlier Section 15 process still applies.

dispute_summary: For appendix disputes, either party may request a new or modified appendix in writing, and if no agreement is reached within 180 days either may initiate Section 15 dispute resolution, where an arbitration under Section 15(c) is conducted before a single neutral arbitrator selected by CPR in a last best offer format; the general Section 15 procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: Neither excerpt set shows the arbitration or court process of the dispute-resolution section. The 2003 excerpt has only a definition and a list of ordinance requirements (subsection (D)), and the 2021 excerpt has the same kind of material, so no comparison is possible.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 Agreement to Amend amends listed definitions and compact sections and does not list Section 15. It states that a dispute under the agreement is resolved under the compact's Section 15 dispute provisions, which therefore continue to apply.

The 2009 Agreement lists the compact sections it amends, and paragraph 11 states that compact provisions not amended by the agreement include the dispute-resolution provisions in Section 15. Section 15 therefore continues to apply.

dispute_summary: For appendix disputes, either party may request a new or modified appendix in writing, and if no agreement is reached within 180 days either may initiate Section 15 dispute resolution, where an arbitration under Section 15(c) is conducted before a single neutral arbitrator selected by CPR in a last best offer format; the general Section 15 procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: Neither excerpt set shows the arbitration or court process of the dispute-resolution section. The 2003 excerpt has only a definition and a list of ordinance requirements (subsection (D)), and the 2021 excerpt has the same kind of material, so no comparison is possible.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 Agreement to Amend amends listed definitions and compact sections and does not list Section 15. It states that a dispute under the agreement is resolved under the compact's Section 15 dispute provisions, which therefore continue to apply.

dispute_summary: Disputes begin with a written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days; either party may then seek arbitration before a single American Arbitration Association arbitrator, but neither party is required to agree to arbitrate, and unresolved disputes may go to the federal district court for the Gaming Facility's district or a state court in San Bernardino County; an arbitrator's decision, if arbitration is used, is binding.

The asserting party serves written notice and representatives meet within thirty days; either party may then refer the dispute to arbitration under AAA rules before one arbitrator, and either party may seek de novo review of the award in federal district court, with the parties waiving immunity for those limited purposes.

dispute_change_summary: The 2018 excerpt is the Interior approval letter and an Oklahoma enrolled act on gaming, not the supplement's dispute terms. The 2007 compact's Part 12 is in the excerpt, so the comparison cannot be made.

dispute_summary: For appendix disputes, either party may request a new or modified appendix in writing, and if no agreement is reached within 180 days either may initiate Section 15 dispute resolution, where an arbitration under Section 15(c) is conducted before a single neutral arbitrator selected by CPR in a last best offer format; the general Section 15 procedure is not in the excerpt.
Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 Agreement to Amend amends listed definitions and compact sections and does not list Section 15. It states that a dispute under the agreement is resolved under the compact's Section 15 dispute provisions, which therefore continue to apply.

dispute_summary: Section 10 provides that if a tribal government bound by the consent judgment breaches it or the compact, the State directs any legal action only at the breaching tribal government and that action does not affect the other valid compacts.

Disputes start with written notice and a 30-day meeting; if the State's claim is not resolved within 90 days, the State may serve notice to stop the disputed games, and the Tribe may stop them or invoke arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration rules while the games continue; the excerpt does not say whether the award binds.

Under Section 9.6, disputes over regulations proceed, when demanded, before a single retired-judge arbitrator under the JAMS Comprehensive Arbitration Rules (or closest equivalent), who selects one party's proposed regulation in an order with review waived, and the Tribe waives sovereign immunity for arbitral enforcement; patron disputes under Section 10.0 go to binding arbitration before a retired judge.

dispute_change_summary: The 2018 amendment repeals and replaces Section 3.1(c), Section 12.6(a) and Section 18.3 and adds Section 18.8, and does not list the arbitration provisions of Section 9. The 2011 Section 9.6 JAMS arbitration therefore still applies.

dispute_summary: Disputes start with written notice and a 30-day meeting; if the State's claim is not resolved within 90 days, the State may serve notice to stop the disputed games, and the Tribe may stop them or invoke arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration rules while the games continue; the excerpt does not say whether the award binds.

Under the amended compliance-review procedure the parties meet and attempt in good faith to resolve compliance issues, and unresolved disputes are noticed under Section 15 of the compact, whose procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2009 agreement to amend lists the provisions it amends (Sections 2(n), 4(d), 5(i) and (n), 3(m), 3(d), 12(e), 7(g) and 3(d)(8)) and does not list Section 15, so the earlier dispute process still governs. The earlier excerpts cite Section 15 but do not include its text.

dispute_summary: After written notice the Tribal Gaming Office and State Gaming Agency directors meet within ten days, then senior representatives; unresolved disputes go on request to non-binding mediation administered by CPR, and then on demand to binding arbitration before a three-arbitrator panel under CPR rules (last-best-offer format unless opted out, no money damages), with an award final and non-appealable except under 9 U.S.C. 10; the parties keep the right to seek injunctive relief in court, including Arizona Superior Court or the U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact keeps the Section 15 sequence (written notice, negotiation, CPR non-binding mediation, then binding CPR arbitration) and adds a Section 3(b)(3) route: if parties cannot agree on a new or modified appendix within 180 days, either may start Section 15 dispute resolution, and at either party's election the arbitration uses a single CPR-selected arbitrator and a last best offer format. The 2003 compact's Section 15 has the same notice, negotiation, mediation and arbitration steps.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 agreement lists thirteen amended provisions (Sections 2, 3, 6 and a Gaming Facility Annex) and says the parties do not amend any other provision, so Section 15 still governs. Paragraph 12 of the agreement directs disputes under the agreement itself to Section 15.

dispute_summary: The party asserting noncompliance serves written notice, the parties meet within thirty days, and if the dispute is unresolved within ninety days either party may pursue any available remedy; mediation or arbitration is used only by mutual agreement.

dispute_change_summary: The 1999 amendment changes Sections XXVI.B, V.A, XV.H.2, XVI.B.1, XXVII.B, XXXIV, XXXV and XXXVI as numbered in the document, and does not list Section XXIII (Dispute Resolution), so the 1992 process still governs. The text of item 8 is cut off in the excerpt.

dispute_summary: A party serves notice of violation, the parties meet and confer, and if unresolved either party may demand binding arbitration, with the award confirmed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin under the Federal Arbitration Act.
dispute_change_summary: The 2003 Second Amendment replaces the dispute section with written notice of violation, a meet and confer of up to ten days, then binding arbitration before an arbitrator from an agreed list under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and Evidence, with court actions in the Western District of Wisconsin and direct federal court suits for temporary injunctive relief. The 1992 compact provided written notice, a meeting within 30 days, and after 90 days any available remedy, with mediation or arbitration only by mutual agreement.

dispute_summary: Under Section XXIII.D and the intermediate extension clause, Ho-Chunk Nation fee disputes go to last-best-offer arbitration, with each party proposing three arbitrators within seven days, and the arbitrator's decision binding on the parties; the excerpt is OCR-garbled in part.
dispute_change_summary: The 2008 amendment, which presupposes a Section XXIII with an arbitration step that the 1992 text lacks, adds a last best offer arbitration format when the compact requires it or the parties agree: each party proposes three arbitrator candidates within 7 days, the Western District of Wisconsin court or JAMS appoints if they cannot agree, and the arbitrator picks one party's final offer within 120 days. The 1992 compact provided notice, a meeting within 30 days, and after 90 days any available remedy, with mediation or arbitration only by mutual agreement.

dispute_summary: Disputes over proposed internal control standards not tied to event wagering go to a single arbitrator sitting in Madison under AAA rules (but not administered by the AAA), who must choose one party's proposal within 30 days.
dispute_change_summary: The 2025 amendment keeps a dispute section (renumbered XXIV) and reopens it with 'Except as otherwise provided in this Compact', and adds a separate arbitration process for proposed MICS amendments not tied to event or remote wagering (Madison, single arbitrator who is a CPA, AAA-type rules, written decision in 30 days choosing one party's proposal). The 1992 compact already had a dispute clause: notice, a meeting within 30 days, and after 90 days any available remedy, with mediation or arbitration only by mutual agreement.

dispute_summary: Disputes over whether the Commission has unreasonably withheld consent to satellite wagering may be taken to arbitration under Section XII.C of the compact, which the excerpt does not contain.
Disputes under the Appendix are resolved under any dispute provisions made applicable in the Appendix, and otherwise under the Compact's dispute provisions, which are not reproduced in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2007 Second Amendment adds Appendix X2 (tribal lottery systems) and does not amend the compact's dispute clause. The appendix only routes disputes: Section 17 sends them to any dispute provisions made applicable in the appendix, or otherwise to the compact's provisions, and Section 3.6.4 sends tribal-versus-state agency disputes to the compact's process. The 2001 compact's Section XII.C (written notice, a meeting within 10 days, then AAA arbitration after 20 days) stays in place.

dispute_summary: Disputes over the addendum terms, including the number of player terminals, must be met on at least 30 days before the increased allocation, and if no resolution is reached either party may use the Compact's dispute provisions.
dispute_change_summary: The 2015 Third Amendment's Appendix X2 Addendum has a dispute clause requiring the parties to meet and confer, then sending unresolved disputes to the Compact's dispute resolution provisions; the earlier excerpts show no dispute clause, so the earlier process cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a good-faith meeting within 10 days and, if unresolved after 30 days, optional arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules with a binding award; otherwise the dispute may go to the U.S. District Court where the gaming facility is located and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, or to state courts if federal courts lack jurisdiction.

If no intergovernmental agreement with the State on a Project is reached within seventy-five days, either party may demand binding JAMS arbitration, and the arbitrator must select one of the two offers.
dispute_change_summary: The earlier compact's Section 9 sets a meet-and-confer step, then optional arbitration, then federal or state court; the replacement excerpts do not show its general dispute section, and the only arbitration shown (Section 11.7) covers disputes over an intergovernmental agreement for off-reservation projects, so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Under Section 15, negotiation followed by mediation and arbitration are the preferred dispute methods, with a court of competent jurisdiction for injunctive relief, which is the Arizona Superior Court for a Native nation claim against the State and the U.S. District Court for Arizona for a State claim.

Disputes go through written notice, a meeting within ten days and thirty days of negotiation, then binding arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules, with federal or state court available to enforce.

dispute_change_summary: The Secretarial Procedures contain no process for disputes between the Native nation and the State (Section 12.0 is reserved, and the only dispute provisions cover patron disputes and a tribal labor ordinance), and they declare prior tribal-state compacts null and void. The 2000 compact's Section 9.0 provided written notice, a meet and confer within 10 days, optional arbitration under AAA rules after 30 days, and federal or state court.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting within ten days, and arbitration in Arizona if the dispute is not resolved within thirty days, with one agreed arbitrator or a panel of three whose third member the American Arbitration Association appoints if the two cannot agree; the majority decision is final, binding and unappealable, and U.S. District Courts have jurisdiction over actions to enjoin class III gaming in violation of the compact.

dispute_change_summary: The earlier Section 15 gives notice, a 10-day meet-and-confer, then binding arbitration in Arizona after 30 days, with a federal-court injunction right; the replacement excerpts do not show its Section 15, though its transfer provisions say a Tribal dispute over a denied transfer is resolved under Section 15, so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Under the amended compliance-review procedure the parties meet and attempt in good faith to resolve compliance issues, and unresolved disputes are noticed under Section 15 of the compact, whose procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The amendment lists nine provisions it amends (Sections 2(n), 4(d), 5(i) and (n), 3(m), 3(d), 12(e), 7(g), 3(d)(8) and 6), and says the Compact's dispute resolution provisions in Section 15 are incorporated; Section 15 is not among the amended provisions, so the earlier Section 15 still governs, but Section 3(d), which contains a Section 15 cross-reference, is amended in part.

dispute_summary: For appendix disputes, either party may request a new or modified appendix in writing, and if no agreement is reached within 180 days either may initiate Section 15 dispute resolution, where an arbitration under Section 15(c) is conducted before a single neutral arbitrator selected by CPR in a last best offer format; the general Section 15 procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2021 compact provides that appendix-related Section 15(c) arbitration is to be conducted before a single neutral selected by CPR under a last-best-offer format; the 2003 Section 15 arbitration text is not in the excerpts (the earlier excerpt only cross-refers to Section 15), so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 amendment lists thirteen provisions it amends (definitions and Sections 3 and 6(b) and an annex) and does not list Section 15; paragraph 12 says disputes under the Agreement use the Compact's Section 15 dispute resolution provisions, so the existing Section 15 still governs.

dispute_summary: Disputes go through written notice, a meeting within ten days and thirty days of negotiation, then binding arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules, with federal or state court available to enforce.

Disputes under the compact begin with a written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days; if unresolved either party may seek arbitration before JAMS, but neither party is required to agree to arbitrate, and unresolved disputes may be brought in the federal district court for the district of the Gaming Facility or, if that court lacks jurisdiction, a state court of competent jurisdiction in the county.

Arbitration is started by written notice under Section 30, each side names a nominee, and the American Arbitration Society names a third arbitrator if the two cannot agree; the excerpt does not say whether awards are binding.

dispute_change_summary: The 1995 compact's dispute section provides for arbitration by one or three arbitrators, a binding decision, and enforcement in the federal court for Kansas; the 2026 amendment's excerpt cuts off after its Section 5 changes, so whether it amends the dispute provisions cannot be seen.

dispute_summary: A party asserting noncompliance serves written notice and the parties' representatives meet within thirty days; either party may then refer the dispute to arbitration under American Arbitration Association rules before one arbitrator, remedies are limited to enforcement of the compact, and either party may seek de novo review of the award in federal district court.

dispute_change_summary: The 2018 supplement adds a non-house-banked table games term and says the games are treated as conducted under the Compact for enforcement and exclusivity; it does not list any compact provision as amended, so the 2005 dispute provisions appear to still govern. The 2005 dispute text is not in the excerpts.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting within 30 days, non-binding arbitration after 60 days with a third arbitrator named by the American Arbitration Association if the two named arbitrators cannot agree, and a declaratory judgment action in the United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma.

The excerpt refers to arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules (subsections 17.2.10.2 to 17.2.10.5) and to an arbitral tribunal under subsection 17.2.10 when a court declines jurisdiction over a Jackson Band proceeding, but the subsections setting out the steps are not in the excerpt.

The compact provides for written notice, a good-faith meeting within 10 days and, if unresolved after 30 days, optional arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules with a binding award; otherwise the dispute may go to the U.S. District Court where the gaming facility is located and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, or to state courts if federal courts lack jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The 2000 compact's Section 9 sets meet-and-confer, arbitration under the AAA Commercial Rules with a neutral or three-member panel, and court action in federal or state court; the 1998 dispute article is not in the excerpts, though the 1998 text refers to binding arbitration under subsection 17.2.10, so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Disputes over which regulation to adopt go to a single retired-judge JAMS arbitrator under Comprehensive Arbitration Rules, whose order takes effect on issuance with review waived; the general Section 13 dispute clause is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2000 compact's Section 9.0 sets meet-and-confer, AAA Commercial Rules arbitration and court action; the 2015 excerpts show a different JAMS arbitration under Section 9.6, under which a retired-judge arbitrator chooses between two proposed regulations, but not the 2015 general dispute article, so the two general processes cannot be compared.

The First Amendment repeals and replaces Compact Sections 5.2(a), 5.2(b) and 5.3 (revenue sharing and credits) and does not list the dispute provisions, so the 2015 dispute provisions appear to still govern.

dispute_summary: Disputes go through written notice and a meet-and-confer within ten days, then the parties may resolve the dispute by JAMS arbitration (JAMS final and unappealable), with remedies otherwise preserved.

Disputes over whether phase-two conditions are met go through the dispute resolution procedures in Section XII of the compact, and the Tribe may not expand gaming stations while that dispute is pending.
dispute_change_summary: The 1995 amendment does not replace Section XII; it sends disputes over the phase-two conditions to the procedures in Section XII, so the 1993 Section XII (agency meet-and-confer, then JAMS arbitration where the compact provides for it, with court remedies preserved) still governs.
The Third Amendment changes only Section IV.A.1(a) (adding Tribal Lottery Systems) and adds Appendix X; it does not list the dispute provisions, so the 1993 Section XII still governs.

The Fourth Amendment adds Appendix X2 as a fully enforceable part of the Compact and recognizes the Tribal Lottery Systems it describes; it does not list the dispute provisions, so the 1993 Section XII still governs, though Appendix X2 itself is not in the excerpts and may contain its own terms.

The Fifth Amendment adds a route for cost-allocation disputes in Appendix X2 Section 13.4.5 (meet and confer within 30 days, then the dispute resolution provisions of Appendix X2 Section 13.5); the 1993 Compact's Section XII is not listed as amended, but Section 13.5 is not in the excerpts, so the full dispute process cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Disputes go through written notice and a meet-and-confer within twenty business days, then optional formal mediation, then standard arbitration by mutual agreement with a decision within one year of the request; judicial resolution remains available if mediation does not resolve the dispute.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides written notice, a meet and confer within 20 business days, optional formal mediation by agreement, judicial resolution if a party is dissatisfied, and arbitration only by mutual agreement (alternating sites, decision within one year, subject to judicial review). The 1993 compact provided notice, a meeting within 10 days, and after 20 more days arbitration through JAMS by agreement or the Section XIII remedies.

dispute_summary: For sports wagering certification, the Tribal and State Gaming Agencies meet and confer on the State Gaming Agency's concerns, and the Tribal Gaming Agency may revoke its approval if it finds the certification was erroneous.
dispute_change_summary: The Seventh Amendment lists its changes (Compact Sections II, III.G, IV.A, XII.D, a digital-wallet clause, a start-up costs fee and a new Appendix S for sports wagering) and does not list Section XIV, so the 2017 dispute process appears to still govern; the excerpts under the dispute heading are Appendix S sports-wagering text.

dispute_summary: Civil disputes arising from the conduct of gaming under the Gaming Code may be heard in the Northwest Intertribal Court, the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribal Court, or an administrative forum; the excerpt does not describe steps between the nation and the State.
dispute_change_summary: The Eighth Amendment rewrites Compact Section XII.B(2) so that civil disputes arising from gaming under the Gaming Code may be heard in the Northwest Intertribal Court, the Jamestown S'Klallam Tribal Court, or an administrative forum; the earlier text of XII.B(2) is not in the excerpts, and the 2017 Section XIV dispute process is not listed as amended, so the two cannot be fully compared.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a good-faith meeting within 10 days and, if unresolved after 30 days, optional arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules with a binding award; otherwise the dispute may go to the U.S. District Court where the gaming facility is located and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, or to state courts if federal courts lack jurisdiction.

Disputes under the compact begin with a written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days; if unresolved either party may seek arbitration before JAMS, but neither party is required to agree to arbitrate, and unresolved disputes may be brought in the federal district court for the district of the Gaming Facility or, if that court lacks jurisdiction, a state court of competent jurisdiction in the county. Sec. 13.4 limits remedies to injunctive relief, specific performance and declaratory relief.
dispute_change_summary: The 2000 compact's Section 9.0 sets meet-and-confer, AAA Commercial Rules arbitration and court action; the 2016 excerpts do not show the replacement's general dispute article (they show a cross-reference to a '13.0 dispute resolution provisions' and safety text), so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting of State and Native nation representatives within thirty days, and a ninety-day period before a notice to cease disputed gaming may be served; the excerpt ends before the arbitration and court steps.

The compact provides for written notice and a response period, then arbitration under the Commercial Arbitration Rules of the American Arbitration Association with attorney arbitrators, and the results are enforceable by an action for injunctive relief in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: Section 7 of both compacts has the same opening steps (written notice, a 30-day meeting, then a 90-day period leading to a notice to cease the disputed game); the 1997 Section 7 adds arbitration under the AAA Commercial Rules by New Mexico-bar attorney arbitrators, with enforcement by injunction in any court. The 1995 excerpt ends before the matching arbitration step, so whether the 1995 compact had the same arbitration terms cannot be seen.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a twenty-day period, and a notice to cease disputed games, after which the responding party may stop the games or invoke arbitration before attorney arbitrators, with the American Arbitration Association choosing any unchosen third arbitrator, and the results are final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The 2002 compact shortens the periods in Section 7: a complaining party may serve a notice to cease the game after 20 days (earlier 90 days), and the responding party must stop or invoke arbitration within 10 days (earlier 30 days). It also drops the earlier required meeting of State and Tribe representatives within 30 days of the notice, adds discovery and open-or-closed hearing rules for the three-attorney AAA arbitration, bars the arbitrators from ruling on the compact's validity, and states that results are final and binding.

dispute_summary: After written notice and a twenty-day period, the complaining party may issue a notice to cease the disputed activity, and either side may invoke arbitration before a three-member panel with the American Arbitration Association appointing a third arbitrator if needed; the arbitration result is final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The 2015 compact keeps the 20-day notice period, the 10-day response and three-attorney arbitration, and adds a two-year window to start the procedure (and a two-year window for the State to raise pre-effective-date payment breaches), allows a single arbitrator by written agreement, sets 30-day periods for choosing arbitrators (a non-responding party is bound to proceed with the other's single arbitrator), and lengthens the third-arbitrator period from 10 to 30 days.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting within ten days, and arbitration in Arizona if the dispute is not resolved within thirty days, with one agreed arbitrator or a panel of three whose third member the American Arbitration Association appoints if the two cannot agree; the majority decision is final, binding and unappealable, and U.S. District Courts have jurisdiction over actions to enjoin class III gaming in violation of the compact.

dispute_change_summary: The 1994 Section 15 gives notice, a 10-day meeting, then arbitration in Arizona after 30 days (AAA appointment of a third arbitrator, binding decision) and a federal-court injunction right; the 2003 excerpts do not show its Section 15, though its transfer provisions refer a Tribal dispute over a denied transfer to Section 15, so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: For appendix disputes, either party may request a new or modified appendix in writing, and if no agreement is reached within 180 days either may initiate Section 15 dispute resolution, where an arbitration under Section 15(c) is conducted before a single neutral arbitrator selected by CPR in a last best offer format; the general Section 15 procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2021 compact says arbitration of appendix disputes under its Section 15(c) is to be before a single neutral selected by CPR under a last-best-offer format, and that either party may start Section 15 dispute resolution if an appendix is not agreed within 180 days; the 2003 Section 15 text is not in the excerpts (the earlier excerpt only cross-refers to it), so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 amendment lists thirteen provisions it amends (definitions, Sections 3 and 6(b), and an annex) and does not list Section 15; paragraph 12 says disputes under the Agreement use the Compact's Section 15 dispute resolution provisions, so the existing Section 15 still governs.

dispute_summary: Disputes under Appendix X are resolved under any dispute provisions made specifically applicable in the Appendix, and otherwise under the binding arbitration provisions of the compact.
dispute_change_summary: The 1999 First Amendment adds Appendix X (Tribal Lottery Systems) with its own Section 16, which resolves disputes under the dispute provisions made applicable in that appendix or, if there are none, under the Compact's binding arbitration provisions; the 1998 compact's dispute article is not in the excerpts, so whether this is a new process cannot be confirmed.

dispute_summary: Disputes under Appendix X2 are resolved under any dispute provision made specifically applicable in the Appendix, otherwise under the compact's dispute provisions, which are not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2007 Second Amendment adds Appendix X2, whose Section 17 routes disputes under that appendix to its own dispute provisions or, if none, to the Compact's Dispute Resolution provisions; the 1998 compact's dispute article is not in the excerpts, so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: The parties meet and attempt to resolve a dispute about Player Terminal allocation not later than 30 days before the increase takes effect; if no resolution is reached, either or both parties may use the dispute resolution provisions of the compact (not in the excerpt).
dispute_change_summary: The 2015 Third Amendment's Appendix X2 Addendum (Section 4) says disputes about the Addendum terms are first met and conferred on and then go to the dispute resolution provisions of the Compact; the 1998 compact's dispute article is not in the excerpts, so the two cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: After written notice and a twenty-day period, the complaining party may issue a notice to cease the disputed activity, and either side may invoke arbitration before a three-member panel with the American Arbitration Association appointing a third arbitrator if needed; the arbitration result is final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The 2015 compact adds a two-year window to start the Section 7 procedure (and a two-year window from the effective date for the State to raise pre-effective-date payment breaches), lets the parties agree in writing to a single arbitrator, sets 30-day periods for choosing arbitrators (if the responding party does not choose, the arbitration goes ahead with the single arbitrator picked by the noticing party), and lengthens the third-arbitrator period from 10 to 30 days.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting of the Governor and Tribal Chief within 30 days, non-binding arbitration after 60 days with a third arbitrator named by the American Arbitration Association if needed, and suit for breach in the United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma.

The parties first give written notice and the Governor and tribal chief meet within thirty days; if unresolved, either party may refer the dispute to non-binding arbitration with the arbitrators named by the parties and, if needed, the American Arbitration Association, and either party may then seek a declaratory judgment in the United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma.
dispute_change_summary: The 1996 compact renumbers the dispute section from 14 to 15, shortens the period before either party may refer a dispute to non-binding three-arbitrator arbitration from 60 days of notice to 30 days, and recasts the court step from a suit for breach to a declaratory judgment action by a party aggrieved by the arbitration decision, in the Western District of Oklahoma. The 30-day meeting of the Governor and Tribal Chief and the sanctions for improper claims are the same.

dispute_summary: Disputes start with written notice and a meeting of tribal and state representatives within thirty days, then either party may refer the dispute to arbitration under AAA rules, and an award may be reviewed de novo by a federal district court whose decision is subject to appeal.
dispute_change_summary: The 2005 compact provides written notice, a meeting within 30 days, and then arbitration that either party may refer to the American Arbitration Association before one arbitrator chosen from an AAA list, limited to enforcement of the compact, with de novo review of the award in federal district court. The 1996 compact provided a 30-day meeting, then non-binding arbitration by a party-named three-member panel after 30 days, and a declaratory judgment action in the Western District of Oklahoma.

dispute_summary: Disputes go through written notice, a meeting within ten days and thirty days of negotiation, then binding AAA commercial arbitration, with federal or state court available to enforce.

dispute_change_summary: The 2024 addendum's Section 4.0 is headed 'Enforcement and Disputes' but its text in the file contains only inspection rights (4.1), and the approval letter says the compact includes dispute resolution provisions that are not in the excerpts, so no dispute process can be compared.

dispute_summary: After written notice, the Governor and the Tribal Chief meet within 30 days; if the dispute is unresolved within 90 days, arbitration decides it, with a third arbitrator appointed by the American Arbitration Association if needed, and the decision is final and non-reviewable; enforcement suits go to the United States District Court, then to state courts if federal jurisdiction is lacking.

dispute_change_summary: The 1994 amendment recites that it makes technical amendments to Sections 6.3, 8.3, 8.8 and the slot game provisions and does not list Section 10 among them, so the 1993 arbitration process still applies.
The 1996 Amendment II recites that it amends only Section 7.6(2) on Class III net revenues and does not list Section 10, so the 1993 arbitration process still applies.

dispute_summary: After a written default notice, the party in default has ninety days to correct; if not, the parties meet within thirty days, and if still unresolved either party may pursue any lawful remedy, including a federal action under 25 U.S.C. 2710(d)(7)(A); the parties may also agree in writing to mediation or arbitration.

After written notice of a substantial default the other party has ninety days to cure, the parties meet within thirty days, and if the dispute is still unresolved within thirty days after that either party may pursue any lawful remedy, including an IGRA section 11(d)(7)(A) action; mediation or arbitration is available only by mutual written agreement.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact keeps Section VIII (the Tribe has jurisdiction over patron disputes, with optional State technical assistance on slot machines) and Section XI.1 on default (written notice, a 90-day cure period, a meeting within 30 days, then any lawful remedy, with mediation or arbitration only by mutual written agreement) in the same terms.

dispute_summary: The parties first give written notice and the Governor and tribal chief meet within thirty days; if unresolved, either party may refer the dispute to non-binding arbitration with the arbitrators named by the parties and, if needed, the American Arbitration Association, and either party may then seek a declaratory judgment in the United States District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma.

Disputes start with written notice and a meeting of tribal and state representatives within thirty days, then either party may refer the dispute to arbitration under AAA rules, and an award may be reviewed de novo by a federal district court whose decision is subject to appeal.
dispute_change_summary: The 2005 compact provides written notice, a meeting within 30 days, and then arbitration that either party may refer to the American Arbitration Association before one arbitrator chosen from an AAA list, limited to enforcement of the compact, with de novo review of the award in federal district court. The 1996 compact provided a 30-day meeting, then non-binding arbitration by a party-named three-member panel after 30 days, and a declaratory judgment action in the Western District of Oklahoma.

The 2019 Supplement accepts additional covered games and states that the non-house-banked table games are subject to the Compact's enforcement and exclusivity provisions. It does not list Part 12, so the 2005 dispute process still applies.

dispute_summary: The State gaming agency delivers a notice of non-compliance and, if the Native nation's operation does not correct it, may sue in U.S. District Court to enjoin the gaming activity; a narrower table-game supervisory-staffing disagreement goes to binding American Arbitration Association arbitration after the parties confer, and Sec. 10(c) routes certain appeals to AAA arbitration if the Connecticut Superior Court lacks jurisdiction.

dispute_change_summary: The 1994 dispute excerpts are wire-transfer and cash-equivalent procedures, not the compact's dispute section. The 2021 amendment excerpts do not show a dispute section either, so neither side's dispute process can be compared.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a good-faith meeting within 10 days and, if unresolved after 30 days, optional arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules with a binding award; otherwise the dispute may go to the U.S. District Court where the gaming facility is located and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, or to state courts if federal courts lack jurisdiction.

Disputes under the compact begin with a written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days; if unresolved either party may seek arbitration before JAMS, but neither party is required to agree to arbitrate, and unresolved disputes may be brought in the federal district court for the district of the Gaming Facility or, if that court lacks jurisdiction, a state court of competent jurisdiction in the county.
dispute_change_summary: The 2000 Section 9 sets a meet-and-confer process and a 30-day period. The 2020 excerpts show a project-related JAMS arbitration in Section 11.11 and an appendix listing a patron disputes ordinance, but no compact-level dispute section, so the change cannot be fully determined.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a good-faith meeting within 10 days and, if unresolved after 30 days, optional arbitration under the AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules with a binding award; otherwise the dispute may go to the U.S. District Court where the gaming facility is located and the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, or to state courts if federal courts lack jurisdiction.

dispute_change_summary: The 2007 amended compact leaves Section 9.0 in place as the general process (the later text refers to 'Amended Compact Section 9.0' for payment and fire-safety disputes) and adds, for failure to remit specified payments, a right for the State to seek injunctive relief immediately in federal or state court notwithstanding Section 9.0, with the Tribe consenting to suit; it also adds JAMS arbitration for patron disputes and for off-reservation mitigation disputes with a county. The 2000 compact's Section 9.0 provided written notice, a meet and confer within 10 days, optional arbitration under AAA rules after 30 days, and then federal or state court.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the compact begin with a written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days; if unresolved either party may seek arbitration before JAMS, but neither party is required to agree to arbitrate, and unresolved disputes may be brought in the federal district court for the district of the Gaming Facility or, if that court lacks jurisdiction, a state court of competent jurisdiction in the county. Sec. 13.4 limits remedies to injunctive relief, specific performance and declaratory relief.
dispute_change_summary: The 2000 Section 9 sets a meet-and-confer process. The 2018 replacement's visible dispute text is a project-related JAMS arbitration in Section 11.8 and a fire-inspector enforcement clause; the compact-level dispute section is not in the excerpts.

dispute_summary: Disputes go through written notice and a meet-and-confer within ten days; if unresolved within twenty days, a party may seek resolution by AAA commercial arbitration at alternating sites, and the arbitrator's decision is final and unappealable; other remedies are preserved.

Disputes over the phase-two conditions go to Section XII.C of the compact, and while the dispute is pending the Tribe may not expand gaming stations, hours or wager limits; the text of Section XII.C is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The visible amendment text does not restate Section XII.C; it refers to that section for disputes over the phase-two conditions and bars gaming expansion while that process runs, but the cut-off text does not show whether XII.C itself is amended.

dispute_summary: Disputes are resolved under any dispute provisions in the Appendix or, if there are none, under the binding arbitration provisions of the Compact; the excerpt does not name an arbitration body or rules.
dispute_change_summary: The 1999 Second Amendment adds Appendix X (tribal lottery systems) without amending Section XII.C. Appendix Section 16 only routes disputes under the appendix to any procedures the appendix makes applicable, or otherwise to the compact's binding arbitration provisions. The 1993 clause (written notice, a meeting within 10 days, then AAA arbitration after 20 days, final and unappealable) stays in place.
The excerpts do not show whether Section XII.C was amended: the visible amendment list covers Sections II and III only, and the text is cut off before any further amended sections.

dispute_summary: Disputes under Appendix X2 are resolved under any dispute provisions in the Appendix or otherwise under the Dispute Resolution provisions of the Compact, which the excerpt does not reproduce.
dispute_change_summary: The 2007 Fourth Amendment adds Appendix X2 (tribal lottery systems) without amending Section XII.C. Appendix Section 17 only routes disputes under the appendix to its own provisions or otherwise to the compact's Dispute Resolution provisions. The 1993 clause (written notice, a meeting within 10 days, then AAA arbitration after 20 days) stays in place.

dispute_summary: The State and Tribe must meet and attempt to resolve disputes over the Addendum terms, and if they cannot reach agreement either party may use the dispute resolution provisions of the Compact, which the excerpt does not reproduce.
dispute_change_summary: The 2019 Fifth Amendment's addendum adds a step for disputes over its terms, such as the number of player terminals: the State and Tribe must meet and attempt to resolve the dispute not later than 30 days before an increased allocation takes effect, and then either may use the compact's dispute resolution provisions. The 1993 Section XII.C (notice, a meeting within 10 days, then AAA arbitration) is not amended.

The excerpts under the dispute heading are Appendix S sports-wagering certification and integrity text, not the Compact's dispute clause, and the amendment's list of changes is cut off before any change to Section XII would appear.

dispute_summary: Either party gives written notice, the parties meet and confer within ten days, and if unresolved either party may seek arbitration under AAA Commercial Rules, whose decision is final and unappealable; mediation is available only by mutual agreement.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact's Section XII.C has the same six dispute steps as the earlier compact: written notice, meet and confer within ten days, AAA commercial arbitration within twenty days of the first meeting, a hearing within fourteen days of naming the arbitrator, a final decision, and a savings clause.

dispute_summary: A gaming agency that finds non-monetary non-compliance delivers a notice, the other agency has thirty Business Days (extendable by fifteen) to cure, and failing that the requesting agency may sue in U.S. District Court; a failure to pay a monetary amount within five business days is a breach; the parties may agree to another means of dispute resolution.

Under the amended compliance-review procedure the parties meet and attempt in good faith to resolve compliance issues, and unresolved disputes are noticed under Section 15 of the compact, whose procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2008 Agreement amends nine listed provisions and paragraph 4 says no other provision of the Compact is amended; paragraph 11 keeps the Compact's Section 15 dispute provisions in force. The earlier Section 15 text is not in the excerpts.

dispute_summary: For appendix disputes, either party may request a new or modified appendix in writing, and if no agreement is reached within 180 days either may initiate Section 15 dispute resolution, where an arbitration under Section 15(c) is conducted before a single neutral arbitrator selected by CPR in a last best offer format; the general Section 15 procedure is not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The excerpts show neither the 2003 Section 15 nor the 2021 Section 15 dispute text; the 2021 compact refers to Section 15 for disputes over transfers and over new or modified appendices, and says arbitration under Section 15(c) for appendix disputes must use a single CPR-selected neutral and a last-best-offer format.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Agreement go to the dispute resolution provisions of Section 15 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not include.
dispute_change_summary: The 2022 Agreement amends 13 listed provisions and paragraph 4 says no other provision is amended, so Section 15 still governs; paragraph 12 of the Agreement sends disputes under the Agreement to that section. The 2021 Section 15 text is not in the excerpts.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a twenty-day period and a notice to cease disputed games, then arbitration by attorney arbitrators with the American Arbitration Association choosing any unchosen third arbitrator; the results are final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.

After written notice and a twenty-day period, the complaining party may issue a notice to cease the disputed activity, and either side may invoke arbitration before a three-member panel with the American Arbitration Association appointing a third arbitrator if needed; the arbitration result is final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The 2015 compact keeps the notice, stop-or-arbitrate election and final and binding attorney arbitration, and adds a two-year window to start the procedure (and a two-year State window for pre-effective-date payment breaches), lets the parties agree in writing to a single arbitrator, sets 30-day periods for choosing arbitrators (a non-responding party is bound to proceed with the other's single arbitrator), and lengthens the third-arbitrator period from 10 to 30 days.

dispute_summary: After written notice, the State and the Native nation meet within 10 working days; if the dispute is unresolved within 60 days after notice, either party may pursue binding arbitration before three AAA-selected arbitrators (or a single arbitrator by written agreement), who must decide within 120 days with no judicial review.

dispute_change_summary: The 2002 Addendum adds only a new Article 6.4 and does not amend Article 21, so the earlier dispute process still governs; Article 6.4 opens with 'notwithstanding any other provision', which the excerpts do not resolve against Article 21.

The 2008 compact, which covers only operation of the Idaho State Lottery on the reservation, has no dispute resolution article (Articles 1 to 12 and Exhibit A contain none). The 1995 compact's Article 21 provided written notice, a meeting within 10 working days, and after 60 days binding arbitration before a three-member AAA-selected panel, with no judicial review.

dispute_summary: Parties give written notice, meet and confer within ten days, negotiate, then arbitrate under the American Arbitration Association Commercial Rules if the dispute is unresolved within twenty days of the first meeting, with the arbitrator's decision final and unappealable.
Disputes are resolved under any dispute provisions in the Appendix or, if there are none, under the binding arbitration provisions of the Compact, which the excerpt does not detail.

The State and Tribe must meet and attempt to resolve disputes over the Addendum terms, and if they cannot reach agreement either party may use the dispute resolution provisions of the Compact, which the excerpt does not reproduce.

Either party gives written notice, the parties meet and confer within twenty business days, then may seek formal mediation by agreement, and if dissatisfied may seek judicial resolution; arbitration occurs only by mutual agreement.

Parties give written notice, meet and confer within ten days, and after twenty days may proceed to a JAMS hearing in Seattle under JAMS policies supplemented by AAA commercial rules, with the JAMS decision final and unappealable.

dispute_change_summary: The First Amendment's list of amended sections does not include Section 12(c), the JAMS dispute process, but it says Section 7 was amended to set the venue for enforcement actions; the new Section 7 text is not in the excerpts, so its effect on enforcement and venue cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: If the State finds the phase-two conditions are not met, the resulting dispute is resolved under the dispute resolution procedures in Section 12 of the Compact, which the excerpt does not reproduce.
dispute_change_summary: The Second Amendment says it amends only Section III and Section XV, so Section 12 is not amended; Section 3(o) still sends disputes over the phase-two conditions to the Section 12 procedures.

dispute_summary: Disputes under the Appendix are resolved under any dispute provisions in the Appendix or, if there are none, under the binding arbitration provisions of the Compact, which the excerpt does not detail.
dispute_change_summary: The 1999 Third Amendment adds Appendix X (tribal lottery systems) without amending Section 12(c). Appendix Section 16 only routes disputes under the appendix to any procedures the appendix makes applicable, or otherwise to the compact's binding arbitration provisions. The 1992 clause (written notice, a meeting within 10 days, then JAMS arbitration after 20 days, final and unappealable) stays in place.

dispute_summary: For a dispute over a new game, the State and Tribal Gaming Agencies must meet and resolve it before play begins, and the Section 12(c) dispute procedures may be used if necessary, which the excerpt does not reproduce.
dispute_change_summary: The Fourth Amendment's visible list changes Section 2 and Section 3, and its new game provisions send disputes to Section 12(c), which the earlier compact sets out; the amendment's list is cut off, so whether Section 12 itself is amended cannot be seen.

The 2007 Fifth Amendment adds Appendix X2 (tribal lottery systems) without amending Section 12(c). The appendix's Section 17 (legible only in spaced-out OCR) routes appendix disputes to its own provisions or otherwise to the compact's Dispute Resolution provisions, and Section 3.6 covers patron and agency disputes. The 1992 clause (written notice, a meeting within 10 days, then JAMS arbitration after 20 days) stays in place.

dispute_summary: Nooksack and the State meet and confer on disputes about the Addendum, and if no resolution is reached either party may use the Compact's dispute resolution provisions, which are not in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The 2019 Sixth Amendment's addendum adds a step for disputes over its terms, such as the number of player terminals: the State and Tribe must meet and attempt to resolve the dispute not later than 30 days before an increased allocation takes effect, and then either may use the compact's dispute resolution provisions. The 1992 Section 12(c) (notice, a meeting within 10 days, then JAMS arbitration) is not amended.

The Seventh Amendment's visible list changes Sections 3, 6, 9 and 10 and is cut off after item 5, so whether Section 12 is changed cannot be seen; the amendment's new enforcement provisions in Sections 6 and 10 may bear on disputes.
The dispute-heading excerpts are Appendix S sports-wagering text, not the Compact's dispute clause; the Eighth Amendment's visible list is cut off, so whether Section 12 is changed cannot be seen.

dispute_summary: The procedures provide only that patron gaming disputes are resolved under the Northern Arapaho Gaming Code, tribal law and regulations, with review by a person separate from the initial decider; they set out no dispute procedure between the Tribe and a State, and they give no one other than the Tribe or the United States standing to enforce them.

dispute_change_summary: Neither the 2005 procedures nor the 2007 gaming procedures show a dispute-resolution section in the excerpts, so the dispute process cannot be compared.
The 2014 excerpt is the Interior approval letter, which does not describe a dispute process, and the amended procedures' text is not in the excerpt, so the dispute process cannot be compared.
The excerpts show no dispute-resolution clause for either the May 1993 agreement or the December 1993 replacement, so the dispute process cannot be compared.
Neither the 1993 agreement excerpt nor the 1998 renewal shows a dispute-resolution clause; the earlier excerpt stops at Section V.
Neither the 1993 agreement excerpt nor the 1999 Sixth Renewal shows a dispute-resolution clause; the earlier excerpt stops at Section V.
Neither the 1993 agreement excerpt nor the 2002 Eighth Renewal shows a dispute-resolution clause; the earlier excerpt stops at Section V.

dispute_summary: The agreement has no negotiation, arbitration or court process for disputes; its only mechanism is default: a party in substantial and continuing failure may be terminated by the other after ninety days written notice and a failure to cure within ninety days.
dispute_change_summary: The 2002 compact's excerpts show no dispute-resolution clause, and the 1993 excerpt stops at Section V, so the dispute process cannot be compared.
Neither the 2002 excerpts nor the 2007 extension shows a dispute-resolution clause, so the dispute process cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Written notice of default with a ninety-day cure period comes first, after which the non-defaulting party may terminate the agreement; the excerpt names no other step.
dispute_change_summary: The 2013 compact's excerpts stop in Section V, and the 2002 excerpts show no dispute clause, so the dispute process cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Disputes over which regulation to adopt go to a single retired-judge JAMS arbitrator under Comprehensive Arbitration Rules, whose order takes effect on issuance with review waived; the general Section 13 dispute clause is not in the excerpt.

Disputes under these Secretarial Procedures begin with a written notice, a written response within 15 days and a meet-and-confer within 30 days; if unresolved either party may seek arbitration before JAMS, but neither party is required to agree to arbitrate, and unresolved disputes may be brought in the federal district court for the district of the Gaming Facility or, if that court lacks jurisdiction, a state court of competent jurisdiction in the county. Sec. 13.4 limits remedies to injunctive relief, specific performance and declaratory relief.
dispute_change_summary: The 2013 North Fork compact's excerpts show a JAMS arbitration process for disputes over gaming regulations (Sections 9.6 and 9.7), but the 2016 Secretarial Procedures excerpts show only Sections 6.4 and 8.2 to 8.4, so the counterpart provision cannot be compared.

dispute_summary: Section 7 requires written notice, a meeting within thirty days, a ninety-day period, and then arbitration under the American Arbitration Association Commercial Arbitration rules before a three-attorney panel, with each party bearing its own costs.

dispute_change_summary: The 2009 amendment rewrites only Sections 3, 4(M)(5), 12(A) and 12(B), 17 and 18 as shown and says all other provisions remain in effect, so Section 7 (written notice, 30-day meeting, 90-day period, then AAA commercial arbitration with Michigan-licensed arbitrators) still governs; the amendment text is cut off in Section 18.

The 2016 Second Amendment amends only Section 17 and Section 18 as shown and says all other provisions remain in effect, so the 1999 Section 7 dispute process (written notice, 30-day meeting, 90-day period, then AAA commercial arbitration with Michigan-licensed arbitrators) still governs; the amendment text is cut off in Section 18.

dispute_summary: Disagreements over suitability determinations go to a three-member arbitration board, in which one member is chosen by each commission and the third is jointly selected, and either party may appeal the arbitration decision to federal district court if permitted by law.

dispute_change_summary: The 2001 amendment replaces Sections 5, 6, 8.8 to 8.23, 8.9 and 11.3 and adds a Section 12, and does not list Section 7.5, so the earlier three-member binding arbitration of suitability disagreements (with appeal to federal district court if permitted by law) still governs.

dispute_summary: Disagreements over the State's suitability determination go to a three-person binding Arbitration Board, initiated by a notice to the South Dakota Commission on Gaming, and either party may appeal the decision to federal district court if permitted by law.
dispute_change_summary: The 2015 compact keeps the three-member binding Arbitration Board for suitability disagreements and the option to appeal to federal district court if permitted by law, but changes how it is formed and run: the board members are the chairs of the State and Tribal gaming commissions (or designees) plus a third jointly selected gaming-regulation expert whose pay is split, the parties are the two commissions, arbitration starts by filing a Notice with the South Dakota Commission on Gaming, and hearings are open unless the board closes them. The 1993 compact had one member chosen by each commission plus one jointly chosen, appointed to three-year terms. The general clause allowing either party to sue in federal district court is unchanged.

The 2022 amendment rewrites only Sections 3.1, 8.4 and 8.5, so Section 7.5 (three-member binding arbitration of suitability disagreements, with appeal to federal district court if permitted by law) appears to still govern; the amendment does not say so expressly and no 2022 dispute text is in the excerpts.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting of State and Native nation representatives within thirty days, and a ninety-day period before a notice to cease disputed gaming may be served; the excerpt ends before any arbitration or court step.

The compact provides for written notice, a twenty-day period and a notice to cease disputed games, then arbitration by attorney arbitrators with the American Arbitration Association choosing any unchosen third arbitrator; the results are final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides a shorter track: the 30-day meeting of representatives after notice is dropped, the complaining party may serve a notice to cease after 20 days instead of 90, the responding party has 10 days instead of 30 to stop or invoke arbitration, and arbitration results are stated to be final and binding; both versions use three arbitrators under a State/Tribe/third selection and enforce results by injunction.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a twenty-day period and a notice to cease disputed games, then arbitration by attorney arbitrators with the American Arbitration Association choosing any unchosen third arbitrator within thirty days; the results are final and binding and enforceable in any court of competent jurisdiction.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides 30-day deadlines for the noticing party and then the responding party to select their arbitrators, and 30 days (earlier ten) for the third arbitrator to be chosen before the American Arbitration Association selects one; the notice, 20-day, 10-day response and binding-results steps are otherwise the same.

dispute_summary: After written notice and twenty days, the complaining party may issue a notice to cease the disputed activity; the responding party may stop or invoke arbitration before a three-arbitrator panel (third arbitrator named by the American Arbitration Association if needed), and the result is final and binding, enforceable by injunctive action in any court of competent jurisdiction; other available remedies are preserved.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides a two-year limit for invoking the procedure (counted from discovery, with a special rule for pre-compact payment breaches), allows the parties to agree to a single arbitrator, and sets 30-day deadlines for each side's arbitrator and for the third (earlier ten days); the 20-day, 10-day and binding-results steps are the same.

dispute_summary: Before suspending the compact or seeking other remedies for a material breach by the Tribe, the State's Director must give written notice with at least 30 days to cure; the Tribe may seek any remedy at law or equity against the State after its own 30-day notice, and the parties may use non-exclusive alternatives such as arbitration or mediation, binding or not.

If the State fails to comply, the Tribe may seek any legal or equitable remedy after written notice to the Director with at least 30 days to cure; the State may suspend the compact or seek other legal remedies after its own notice; and Section 21.3 allows non-exclusive alternatives such as arbitration or mediation, binding or not, by agreement.
dispute_change_summary: The State-breach remedy (now Section 21.2) and the non-exclusiveness provision (now Section 21.3) read the same as the 1992 Sections 20.2 and 20.3 apart from the section numbers; the Omaha-breach provision (Section 20.1 in 1992) is not in the 1999 excerpt, so it cannot be fully compared.

dispute_summary: For a non-material breach, the party asserting it gives written notice, the parties meet and confer within 15 days, and if unresolved the complaining party may demand a cure within 10 days; if the demand is rejected or ignored, the parties go to AAA Commercial Mediation and then binding arbitration under AAA rules before one or three arbitrators, with the non-prevailing party paying arbitration costs.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact adds Section 20, a binding process for non-material breaches (written notice, a 15-day meet-and-confer, a 10-day response to a demand, American Arbitration Association mediation, then binding arbitration with the non-prevailing party paying costs), and lets either party invoke it for material breaches in place of a 30-day cure-and-terminate notice. The earlier compact let the Director seek any remedy or the Native nation seek any remedy at law or equity after a 30-day notice and cure period, with arbitration or mediation only by mutual agreement.

dispute_summary: After written notice and a thirty-day negotiation period, the parties may elect arbitration or mediation, binding or nonbinding as they choose, and otherwise the dispute goes to the United States District Court for the District of Nebraska.

After notice and a meeting of representatives, disputes not resolved within thirty days go to binding AAA arbitration, and the award may be enforced in the federal court for the Northern District of New York. State claims of unauthorized gaming are not subject to mandatory arbitration.

A party asserting noncompliance serves written notice, the parties meet within thirty days, and if unresolved within ninety days either party may pursue any remedy otherwise available; mediation or arbitration is used only by mutual agreement.

dispute_change_summary: The 1998 amendments change Section V.A, add Section XV.I and new Sections XXXII to XXXIV, and do not list Section XXII (the 1991 dispute procedure: written notice, thirty-day meeting, ninety days, then any available remedy), so the earlier clause still governs; the 1998 excerpt contains no dispute text.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a meeting of the Governor's and the Nation's representatives within twenty days, optional non-binding mediation, and then arbitration by a three-member panel for the listed articles.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact replaces Article XXII: the earlier text had a notice, a meeting within 30 days and, after 90 days without resolution, any available remedy, with ADR only by mutual agreement. The later compact provides negotiation within 20 days of notice, optional non-binding mediation by written agreement, and arbitration by a three-member panel as the sole mechanism for disputes under listed Articles, with demand allowed after 30 days; disputes under Articles IV, XXIII and XXXII are not arbitrable except the Nation's claims for money owed by the State.

The 2021 excerpts show no dispute text, only a renumbering of the dispute articles (the 2003 Article XXIII is now Article XXIV), so the 1992 Article XXII process cannot be compared with the later text.
The 2025 excerpts show no dispute article, so the 1992 Article XXII cannot be compared with the later text.

dispute_summary: The compact provides for written notice, a Governor and Tribal Chief meeting within 30 days, non-binding arbitration after 30 days with an arbitrator named by the American Arbitration Association if needed, and a declaratory judgment action in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Oklahoma.

The compact provides for written notice, a meeting within 30 days, arbitration under American Arbitration Association rules with one arbitrator chosen from an AAA list if the parties cannot agree, and de novo review of any award in federal district court.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides a notice and a 30-day meeting of the Native nation's and State's representatives, then either party may refer any dispute to arbitration before a single AAA-listed arbitrator, with remedies limited to enforcing the compact and de novo review of any award in federal district court. The earlier compact had the same notice and 30-day meeting, then non-binding arbitration with a three-member panel (one named by each party, third by the two or the AAA) and a declaratory-judgment action in the Northern District of Oklahoma, and said the steps did not prevent seeking immediate judicial relief.
The 2018 Non-house-Banked Table Games Supplement states that it is to be governed in accord with the 2005 compact and does not amend Part 12, so the 2005 dispute process still governs.

dispute_summary: Disputes between the Tribe and the State go first to mediation with a mutually agreeable mediator, and if mediation fails, or injunctive relief to prevent irreparable harm is sought, the dispute is litigated in federal court with limited waivers of sovereign immunity; arbitration is not provided for in the excerpt.
dispute_change_summary: The later compact provides a two-step process for disputes between the Native nation and the State: mediation first (unless irreparable harm requires injunctive relief filed directly in federal court), then litigation in federal court with limited waivers of sovereign immunity, and gives the Governor exclusive authority to settle for the State.
